Loving Your Enemies: The Hardest Command
Have you ever had a moment where someone’s words or actions cut so deep, you just wanted to snap back? Maybe a coworker tried to undermine you, or a neighbor spread a nasty rumor. The sting is real, and the anger that bubbles up can feel completely justified. In times like these, the idea of actually loving your enemies? Honestly, it sounds impossible.
But this is right at the heart of what “Strength to Love” is all about. It isn’t saying we should just ignore when we’re hurt, or pretend that pain doesn’t matter. Instead, it’s asking us to see beyond that first wave of anger—to realize that the people who hurt us are often trapped in their own cycles of fear, ignorance, or even suffering.
Picture this: a father sits in his living room, replaying a heated argument with his brother. Sharp words, followed by a heavy silence. He’s tempted to call and demand an apology, to make his brother feel that sting of regret. But then, something his heart remembers: “Hate cannot drive out hate; only love can do that.” Those words hang in the air, softening his anger bit by bit. So instead of calling to accuse, he picks up the phone... and calls to listen.
Most people don’t realize just how much strength it takes to reach out like that. It isn’t about excusing bad behavior, or letting injustice slip by. It’s about refusing to let bitterness take root in your own heart. It means seeing the humanity in the very people who’ve hurt us. And over time, this choice—again and again—can break the cycle of retaliation, opening the door to real healing.
Let me share another story. There was a community divided for years by old wounds. Each side blamed the other, and every attempt at making peace just led to more pain. But then, a small group decided to try something different. They invited their so-called “enemies” to a meal—not to argue, but simply to listen. That first dinner? It was awkward. Old hurts came bubbling up. But as the weeks passed, something shifted. People started seeing each other as neighbors, not adversaries. It wasn’t easy, and not everyone was ready to forgive. But by reaching out—by choosing love over hate—the community began to change from within.
What really stands out here is that loving your enemies isn’t weakness. It’s actually a radical act of courage—a way of refusing to be defined by the worst moments, or by the deepest hurts. It’s like saying, “I won’t let what you did decide who I become.” In a world that often celebrates revenge, this kind of love shines like a beacon of hope.
It’s easy to slip into thinking forgiveness is only for those who deserve it... that reconciliation can only happen if the other person changes first. But here’s something to remember: the first step almost always comes from someone willing to risk vulnerability, to reach across the divide—without any guarantees.
